hero.headline: Palm Beach County Haitians face deportation after Supreme Court eliminates protected status
hero.teaser: The Supreme Court sided with the Trump administration to eliminate Temporary Protected Status for thousands from Haiti and Syria, including 68,400 Haitians in Palm Beach County.
hero.body:
The Supreme Court has sided with President Donald Trump's administration in eliminating Temporary Protected Status for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria. This decision puts hundreds of thousands at immediate risk of deportation, with significant impacts on South Florida. Temporary Protected Status allows foreign citizens already in the United States to remain, work, and support their families while their home countries experience crises such as natural disasters, political unrest, or violence. For Haitians and Syrians, this protection is now ending. The ruling affects approximately 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians nationwide.

Florida is home to the largest Haitian immigrant population in the United States. Within the state, Palm Beach County ranks third with 68,400 Haitian immigrants, behind Miami-Dade County with 78,800 and Broward County with 86,100. Attorney Byrnes Guillaume, who is Haitian and represents many people facing loss of TPS, explains the practical consequences. "It means that they have no status," Guillaume said. "It means that if you have a job you no longer are able to work. It means that you were once legal and now you have to go in the shadow." He raises concerns about families with American-born children: "For people with American-born kids, what you going to do, are you going to leave the kids here or are you going to take them to Haiti, a country they've never known? I do think lives will be at risk."

Stecko Dulcio, who owns a Haitian restaurant in Riviera Beach where he has served cuisine for five and a half years, became a U.S. citizen and considers himself fortunate to have security. He knows many friends with TPS and worries about their prospects. "That's going to be a disaster," Dulcio said. "Not only are their lives in danger, and even if they go they don't get killed, but they're going to have a miserable life, because there's no work, no job, and they lose everything they have." Dulcio notes that gangs have taken control in Haiti, seizing houses, controlling transportation, and perpetuating violence.

The Trump administration argues that TPS was designed as temporary relief during emergencies and that conditions in Haiti and Syria have sufficiently improved to no longer warrant the protection. Advocates strongly dispute this assessment. The Department of Homeland Security maintains it has sole discretion to determine when protections should end. Guillaume said no timeline for deportations has been established. Since January of last year, DHS has ended protections for people from more than 13 countries. Dulcio urges action: "Pray to the government of the United States to do something to help those people."

cards.headline: Martin County water plant crash disrupts service after driver flees scene
cards.teaser: A crash at a Martin County water plant Thursday disrupted water service after the driver fled the scene.
cards.body:
A crash at a Martin County water plant Thursday disrupted water service after the driver fled the scene. The Martin County Sheriff's Office identified the driver who crashed into the water plant facility before leaving the area.

The crash occurred Thursday evening at the Martin County water treatment facility. Officials said the driver left the scene following the collision with the plant infrastructure. Water service to customers was affected by the incident.

Martin County authorities worked to identify and locate the driver who fled after the crash. The collision caused damage to the water plant that required immediate response from county utilities staff. Service disruptions impacted residents supplied by the affected facility.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office successfully identified the driver after investigating the hit and run crash. Officials did not immediately provide details on the extent of damage to the water plant or how long service disruptions would last for affected customers.

cards.headline: Orlando Health opens eight-exam room primary care center in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: Orlando Health held a ribbon cutting Thursday for a new eight-exam room adult primary health care center in Vero Beach.
cards.body:
Orlando Health held a ribbon cutting Thursday for a new eight-exam room adult primary health care center in Vero Beach designed to address primary care shortages in Indian River County. The facility can accommodate 40 patients a day and has opportunity to grow, according to Aaron Bridges, assistant vice president of Orlando Health. The center will be led by husband-and-wife physicians Dr. Meron Kristos and Dr. Gabitto, who met in residency at the former St. Vincent's hospital in New York City. According to the Cleveland Clinic, Indian River County is designated a health professional shortage area and medically underserved area. Kristos told WPTV that primary care access is limited throughout Florida, but "the Vero Beach need really stood out."

Christine Stenback, who moved to Indian River County nearly three decades ago, said the shortage has been a long-standing problem. She and her daughter retained their doctors in Fort Lauderdale and traveled back for specialist care because of limited local options. Kristos noted that patients are waiting months and months for primary care appointments and said the new facility will provide quick timeframes for patients to get established. The Orlando Health Physician Associates Adult Medicine facility is located at 3745 11th Circle Suite 101 in Vero Beach.

cards.headline: DeSantis vetoes bills on e-bike safety tracking and teen poll workers despite unanimous legislative support
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis rejected two bipartisan bills that passed the Legislature with unanimous votes, including one that would have created a statewide system for tracking e-bike and scooter crashes.
cards.body:
Ron DeSantis vetoed Senate Bill 382 and House Bill 461 just before 8 p.m. Thursday, rejecting two bipartisan measures that passed the Legislature with unanimous votes earlier this year. SB 382, filed by Republican Sen. Keith Truenow, sought to create a statewide system for tracking e-bike and scooter crashes. Currently, local and state agencies record these incidents differently, leaving no consistent data for policymakers to assess the scale of the problem. The legislation would have established a task force to deliver recommendations by Oct. 1 on regulating micromobility devices. The bill also aimed to cap e-bike speeds at 10 miles per hour on sidewalks when pedestrians are nearby and require riders to yield on shared paths, with violations treated as non-criminal traffic infractions. DeSantis' veto comes weeks after an Orlando boy was killed on his e-scooter in Lake Nona when the 13-year-old cut in front of a truck while picking up flowers for Mother's Day.

DeSantis also rejected HB 461, which would have allowed high school students to volunteer as poll workers in exchange for community service hours for graduation requirements or Bright Futures scholarships. The bill, sponsored by Republican Reps. Kiyan Michael and Susan Valdés, would have loosened rules on privately funded election-related expenses to allow students to volunteer at polls before the August Primary. The measure was backed by the League of Women Voters and the Southern Poverty Law Center. The Governor additionally vetoed HB 4075, a local bill for the town of Davie in Broward County, sponsored by Democrat Rep. Michael Gottlieb, that would have exempted agricultural land from outdoor advertising laws.

cards.headline: Trump approval rating drops underwater in Florida as midterms approach
cards.teaser: New polling shows 52% of Florida voters now view President Donald Trump unfavorably, compared to 46% who see him positively, a ten-point swing from January.
cards.body:
New polling from Global Strategy Group shows President Donald Trump's approval rating has dropped significantly in Florida. The latest numbers show 52% of Florida voters view Trump unfavorably compared to 46% who view him positively, marking a ten-point swing from January when he held a +4 net approval rating. He now sits at -6. The poll was released by Democratic Senate candidate Alex Vindman's campaign as he argues Florida could be competitive when U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody faces voters in November. According to a GSG polling memo, this double-digit decline in Trump's popularity has created a more favorable political environment for Democrats in 2026.

Trump is losing support within his own base. Since January, support among White college-aged voters has dropped 15 points, while registered Republicans have seen a net 10-point decline in approval. Even among self-identified Trump 2024 voters, his numbers are down 10 points. The trend extends beyond Florida. GSG found Trump's approval underwater in Ohio, where he sits at 41% approval and 53% disapproval, and in Texas at 41% to 54%. In May, the same pollster found Moody holding a 46% to 43% lead over Vindman, within the poll's 3.1% margin of error. For comparison, in 2018, the last midterm during Trump's presidency, exit polls showed he remained popular in Florida despite national unpopularity.

cards.headline: Spirit Airlines bankruptcy leaves Treasure Coast travelers with fewer low-cost flight options
cards.teaser: Spirit Airlines is in bankruptcy court to sell its planes, airport gates and potentially its headquarters, leaving travelers with one fewer budget carrier option.
cards.body:
Spirit Airlines is now in bankruptcy court to sell off everything, including its planes, airport gates and potentially its headquarters. The airline's disappearance means travelers have one fewer low-cost carrier option. For some travelers, the loss is significant. "A lot of people flew Spirit because it was so cost-effective, and everything is so expensive these days, it gave them an option to travel," one traveler told WPTV on Thursday.

A Treasure Coast entrepreneur, LeRoy Gillead II, has proposed buying up all of Spirit, rehiring the airline's workers and rebranding it as Florida Air Express, a low-cost airline based in West Palm Beach. Court papers show Gillead is looking to raise as much as $250 million from private investors. However, Clint Henderson, managing editor of news at The Points Guy travel website, is skeptical. "This seems like a pie in the sky thing. If they can get the money together, maybe they'll establish a new low-cost carrier, but right now they don't fly any routes at all," Henderson said. He expects the airline's assets will instead be divided among the highest bidders, likely major airlines. The deadline for bids comes in July.

cards.headline: Orlando Health opens eight-room primary care center in Vero Beach to ease physician shortage
cards.teaser: Orlando Health opened a new eight-exam room adult primary health care center in Vero Beach on Thursday with a ribbon cutting ceremony.
cards.body:
Orlando Health held a ribbon cutting Thursday for a new eight-exam room adult primary health care center in Vero Beach designed to address physician shortages in Indian River County. The facility, located at 3745 11th Circle Suite 101, can serve 40 patients daily and has room for expansion, according to Aaron Bridges, assistant vice president of Orlando Health. The center will be led by husband-and-wife physicians Dr. Meron Kristos and Dr. Gabitto, who met during residency at the former St. Vincent's hospital in New York City.

Indian River County is designated a health professional shortage area and medically underserved area by the Cleveland Clinic. Dr. Kristos told WPTV that primary care access is limited throughout Florida, but "the Vero Beach need really stood out." Patients in the area are waiting months for appointments due to the shortage. Christine Stenback, who has lived in Indian River County for nearly three decades, said the shortage forced her and her daughter to retain doctors in Fort Lauderdale and travel back for medical care and specialists. Kristos said the new facility aims to provide quick appointment times for established patients and same-day access when health issues arise.

cards.headline: Delray Beach food truck owner calls mother's Venezuela earthquake survival a miracle
cards.teaser: Josney Peroza, who owns Ukelele Foods and operates a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, said his mother survived a building collapse in Venezuela after two powerful earthquakes struck the country.
cards.body:
Josney Peroza, owner of Ukelele Foods Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, learned of two earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes that struck Venezuela seconds apart when news alerts arrived. After someone sent him a video showing the building where his mother lived, his brother confirmed she had been inside when it collapsed. For about eight hours, Peroza did not know if his mother was alive. After 3 a.m., his family received a call saying she was alive but trapped under the rubble. Relatives and neighbors used their bare hands to free her. His mother sustained a broken hip, requires surgery and lost her home.

Peroza said Venezuela lacks the infrastructure to handle a disaster of this magnitude and urgently needs international help. Officials confirm nearly 200 people are dead and at least 1,000 others are hurt. He described the wider humanitarian crisis in La Guaira where survivors have no power, water or homes. When asked if his mother's survival was a miracle, Peroza said "Yeah, it's absolutely a miracle." Rather than traveling to Venezuela, he plans to help his mother from Florida, saying "We don't have any plans to go down there. I think that we are more helpful from here."

cards.headline: Boca Raton psychiatrist license suspended after patients allege he asked them to undress on Zoom
cards.teaser: Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo issued an emergency suspension of Dr. Andrew Sorial's medical license after at least two patients said they were asked to undress during Telehealth sessions.
cards.body:
A Boca Raton psychiatrist is facing serious allegations after at least two patients say they were asked to undress during mental health appointments conducted through Telehealth sessions. Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo issued an emergency suspension of Dr. Andrew Sorial's medical license after the allegations were filed. According to state documents, a 29-year-old patient identified as S.A. began treatment with Sorial in 2020 for depression, anxiety and OCD. During a Zoom appointment, the woman discussed body image concerns when Sorial allegedly asked to assess her body and eventually requested she strip down to a bra and underwear. In another visit, the patient was allegedly asked to take off her top and show him her breasts. State documents include an exchange where Patient S.A. asked Sorial if he was asking her to take her top off and show him her naked breasts, to which Sorial said, "yes, if that's what you're comfortable with."

Around summer of 2025, another patient, a 33-year-old woman identified as C.B., saw Sorial for ADHD, depression and bipolar disorder. State documents allege similar requests over Zoom, escalating to providing photos of the patient in a bra, underwear or bikini. A lawsuit has been filed against Sorial and Boca Raton Psychiatry. WPTV sought a response from Sorial and the practice but did not receive one. No criminal charges have been filed. Palm Beach County Victim Services operates a 24-hour crisis helpline at (561) 833-7273, with a toll-free number at (866) 891-7273 for those outside the local calling area.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach Hanley Center helps veteran overcome eight-year drug addiction
cards.teaser: Chris Claflin, a Harvard Business School graduate and Navy pilot who flew jets in combat, said the Hanley Center in West Palm Beach helped him get more than a year sober after eight years of drug addiction.
cards.body:
Chris Claflin graduated from Harvard Business School and served as a Navy pilot who flew jets in combat, but his success unraveled when he struggled with drug addiction for eight years. Claflin traced the onset of his addiction partly to unresolved trauma from his childhood. He is currently more than a year sober and credits the Hanley Center in West Palm Beach with changing his life for the better.

Now working toward becoming a certified counselor, Claflin has a message for others struggling with addiction, especially veterans. "You can't do this on your own. It's not something you can figure out. Once you get so far down the rabbit hole, you can't pull yourself out on your own," he said. The care he received at the Hanley Center proved instrumental in his recovery and transformation.

hero.headline: Spirit Airlines bankruptcy raises questions about future of low-cost air travel from West Palm Beach
hero.body:
Spirit Airlines is undergoing bankruptcy proceedings to liquidate its assets, including aircraft, airport gates, and potentially its headquarters. The airline's closure removes another budget carrier from the market and raises concerns about the future of affordable air travel options for consumers.

A Treasure Coast entrepreneur named LeRoy Gillead II has submitted a proposal to acquire Spirit Airlines in its entirety, rehire its workforce, and rebrand the company as Florida Air Express, a low-cost airline based in West Palm Beach. According to court documents, Gillead is seeking to raise approximately $250 million from private investors to fund this venture. However, Clint Henderson, managing editor of news at The Points Guy travel website, expressed skepticism about the proposal's likelihood of success. Henderson stated that major airlines will probably acquire Spirit's assets through a bidding process rather than a single buyer establishing a new carrier. The bidding deadline is set for July.

For many travelers, Spirit's disappearance represents a genuine setback. Passengers relied on the airline because of its low fares, which provided an affordable travel option during a period of rising costs across the economy. The airline's distinctive yellow jets have become iconic in the aviation industry. Henderson noted that low-cost carriers are becoming increasingly scarce in the United States, as the budget airline business model struggles to generate profits. He pointed out that Frontier and Allegiant remain in the low-cost category, though options continue to narrow.

Henderson offered practical advice for consumers navigating the changing airline landscape. He recommended that travelers stop being brand-loyal and instead focus on finding the cheapest available fares across all carriers. He suggested using Google Flights to compare prices and encouraged consumers to put effort into researching bargains rather than defaulting to familiar airlines. The aircraft, gates, and other Spirit assets have value to potential buyers, though the airline's signature yellow jets will likely be repainted when transferred to new operators. Henderson summed up the broader trend by saying that the low-cost carrier model in the United States faces fundamental challenges, suggesting travelers should adapt their approach to booking flights by prioritizing price over airline preference.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast entrepreneur proposes buying Spirit Airlines, basing Florida Air Express in West Palm Beach
hero.teaser: LeRoy Gillead II, a Treasure Coast entrepreneur, has proposed buying up all of Spirit Airlines, rehiring the airline's workers and rebranding it as Florida Air Express, a low-cost airline based in West Palm Beach.
hero.body:
A Treasure Coast entrepreneur has put forward a proposal to purchase Spirit Airlines out of bankruptcy and relaunch it as Florida Air Express, a low-cost carrier based in West Palm Beach. LeRoy Gillead II's plan includes rehiring Spirit's workers and keeping the airline operational. According to court filings, Gillead is seeking to raise up to $250 million from private investors to make the purchase. The deadline for bids on Spirit's assets is scheduled for July.

Spirit Airlines is currently in bankruptcy court selling off all of its assets, including aircraft, airport gates, and potentially its headquarters. These components represent significant value in the aviation industry. However, industry experts question whether Gillead's proposal will succeed in the competitive bidding process. Clint Henderson, managing editor of news at The Points Guy travel website, described the plan as "pie in the sky" and predicted a different outcome. "It would be much more likely in the end that you'll see the assets of Spirit divvied out to the highest bidder, and that's probably going to be major airlines," Henderson said.

The collapse of Spirit Airlines marks another loss for budget air travel in the United States. Many travelers relied on the airline because of its affordability at a time when travel costs continue to rise. Henderson noted that the low-cost carrier model is struggling across the industry. "I think the low-cost carrier model is kind of busted in the U.S. All the low-cost carriers really struggle to make money," he said. While Frontier and Allegiant remain in the low-cost category, these carriers face ongoing challenges in maintaining profitability.

For consumers seeking affordable airfare, Henderson recommends taking a different approach to finding deals. Rather than remaining loyal to a single airline, travelers should compare prices across all available options. "Be airline agnostic; that's the best advice I have for consumers. Go with the cheapest airline you can find. Use Google Flights and don't try to be loyal to one airline," he advised. As for Spirit's distinctive yellow aircraft, they will likely be repainted and rebranded by whatever airline or company eventually acquires them.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound under boil water notice after driver crashes into water plant pipe
cards.teaser: A driver crashed into a large pipe at the South Martin Regional Utility's North Water Treatment Plant Wednesday night and fled the scene, leaving about 7,000 residents without water service or adequate water pressure.
cards.body:
A driver crashed into a large pipe at the South Martin Regional Utility's North Water Treatment Plant and fled the scene Wednesday night, leaving about 7,000 residents without water service or adequate water pressure. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says Eliuvar Garza, 24, of Stuart, was speeding when he blew through a stop sign at Osprey Street and Wren Avenue around 9 p.m. He then went through a fence at the water treatment plant, hit a palm tree and broke it in half, then landed on top of a water pipe. A family member later brought Garza to the hospital for his injuries, where deputies found him. According to Sheriff John Budensiek, Garza was disoriented and smelled of alcohol, telling deputies he had consumed two Corona beers. The sheriff noted that Garza has multiple speeding tickets and has never had a driver's license.

South Martin Regional Utility Director Matt Hammond said water utility crews quickly responded and restored water services within two hours. Customers will not be charged for the repairs, which will be submitted as a claim to insurance companies. SMRU has issued a boil water notice for customers who experienced the water shortage, which Hammond said will likely remain in effect through the weekend. Garza faces numerous charges, including leaving the scene of a crash with property damage, driving without a license, failure to use due care, and failure to stop at a stop sign.

cards.headline: Boca Raton George Snow Scholarship Fund awards record $7.5 million to 470 students
cards.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded a record $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County, according to President Tim Snow. The program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford by offering four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college.

The fund's services extend beyond financial assistance. Vice President of Development Jay Brandt noted that GSSF provides mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast. The Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, offers professional, formal, and casual wear, along with footwear and accessories, so scholars can enter interviews, internships, and campus life with confidence. Among 2026 recipients is Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate who earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship. Chow plans to attend Georgetown University.

cards.teaser: West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade offers programs to get people trained and ready to find work in culinary, welding, carpentry and other trades.
cards.body:

The center recently set up at the library in Belle Glade to spread the word about its many programs. Dowdell explained they have programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and much more, all designed to provide certifications that lead to employment opportunities in the area.

cards.headline: Hanley Center in West Palm Beach helps veteran overcome eight years of drug addiction
cards.teaser: Chris Claflin, a Navy pilot who flew jets in combat and graduated from Harvard Business School, received care at the Hanley Center in West Palm Beach that helped him overcome eight years of drug addiction.
cards.body:
Chris Claflin, a Harvard Business School graduate and former Navy pilot who flew jets in combat, struggled with drug addiction for eight years before seeking help at the Hanley Center in West Palm Beach. Claflin traced the onset of his addiction partly to unresolved trauma from his childhood. He is currently more than a year sober and credits the care he received at the Hanley Center with changing his life for the better.

Now working toward becoming a certified counselor, Claflin has a message for others struggling with addiction, particularly veterans. He emphasized that overcoming addiction cannot be done alone, stating that once someone goes too far down that path, they cannot pull themselves out without help. The Hanley Center serves as a resource for supporting the mental health and well-being of service members and others facing similar challenges.

hero.headline: Delray Beach food truck owner calls mother's Venezuela earthquake survival a miracle
hero.teaser: Josney Peroza, who owns Ukelele Foods and operates a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, said his mother survived two powerful earthquakes in Venezuela that measured 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes.
hero.body:
Josney Peroza, owner of Ukelele Foods Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, learned of a devastating disaster when news alerts reported two powerful earthquakes striking his home country seconds apart. The quakes measured 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes and struck the coastal state of La Guaira. When initial images arrived, Peroza saw a video showing the building where his mother lived had collapsed. Hours later, his brother confirmed she had been inside when it fell. For the next eight hours, Peroza could not reach his mother as communication throughout Venezuela shut down due to widespread power outages and severed connections. Around 3 a.m., the family finally received a call confirming his mother was alive but trapped under the rubble. Relatives and neighbors worked with their bare hands to free her from the debris.

Despite her rescue, Peroza's mother faced serious injuries and loss. She sustained a broken hip requiring surgery and lost her home entirely in the collapse. Peroza described the broader humanitarian catastrophe unfolding across the region, where officials confirmed nearly 200 deaths and at least 1,000 injured. The country lacked any infrastructure to handle a disaster of this magnitude, he said. Most buildings in Venezuela are constructed from concrete and metal, making rescue efforts extremely difficult without proper equipment. Residents had been forced to use prayer and their bare hands as their main tools for helping people still trapped in the wreckage.

Peroza emphasized the urgent need for immediate international assistance. He noted that Venezuela had no power, no water, and no shelter for displaced survivors. He described widespread uncertainty about food, housing, and employment in the coming days. The United States announced it would send rescue crews to help. Peroza said he believed he could better assist his mother and his country by remaining in Florida rather than traveling to the disaster zone. From there, he could work toward rebuilding her life and support the broader relief efforts while continuing to operate his food truck.

Peroza described his business as more than a place to eat, calling it "a cultural Venezuelan experience" and "Venezuela without a passport." He planned to continue serving customers while sharing his country's story and helping survivors. He viewed his mother's survival as proof that more lives could still be saved with rapid international response. For those still waiting for word from loved ones in Venezuela, Peroza offered a message of faith and resilience, emphasizing the importance of trusting in the Lord during the crisis.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Zoo announces first-ever koala joey is a boy
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach Zoo revealed Thursday that their first-ever koala joey born on site is a boy. The tiny koala was born in September and has been growing in his mother Elin's pouch for months.
cards.body:
Animal Experience Curator Mike Terrell announced at the koala habitat that the Palm Beach Zoo's first-ever koala joey is a boy. Born in September no bigger than a jelly bean, the joey immediately crawled into his mother Elin's pouch where he has been growing and developing for months. He is now starting to explore outside the pouch and spends most of his time on his mother's back, usually keeping an arm connected to her for safety as he cautiously ventures into the world.

The Palm Beach Zoo has just unveiled an expanded koala habitat featuring a climate-controlled indoor forest with solar tubes for natural lighting and carefully designed perching areas that encourage natural behaviors. The joey is part of a critical conservation program facilitated by San Diego Zoo Global, with koalas in North America on loan from the Australian federal government to support conservation efforts for the endangered species. Zoo visitors will soon witness the joey riding on his mother's back, a milestone expected closer to summer. Every visitor who meets the joey helps support these vital conservation efforts.

cards.headline: Breeze Airways adds 5 new routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport starting at $79
cards.teaser: Breeze Airways announced Wednesday five new routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport with one-way fares starting at $79.
cards.body:
Breeze Airways announced five new routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport on Wednesday, with one-way fares starting at $79. Travelers can book flights to Atlantic City, New Jersey with nonstop service on Mondays and Fridays starting October 2 from $89 one way, and Baltimore with nonstop service on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays starting October 1 from $79 one way. The airline also added Burlington, Vermont and Provo, Utah with one-stop, no-change-of-plane BreezeThru service, plus Trenton, New Jersey with nonstop service on Wednesdays and Saturdays beginning September 30 from $89 one way. The new routes begin between September 30 and October 4.

Breeze, which started operations in 2021, currently operates more than 300 year-round and seasonal routes to 91 cities in the United States, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. Passenger numbers at Vero Beach Regional Airport have seen dramatic growth in the last year. JetBlue began service to Boston and New York's JFK airports in December, and American Airlines began service to Charlotte in February. The airport has increased flight options to serve the Treasure Coast's growing population.

cards.headline: Strong storms topple trees and damage property in Royal Palm Beach and Wellington
cards.teaser: Strong thunderstorms swept through Royal Palm Beach and Wellington Wednesday night, toppling trees, twisting fences and knocking down light poles across both communities.
cards.body:
Strong thunderstorms swept through Royal Palm Beach and Wellington Wednesday night, toppling trees, twisting fences and knocking down light poles across both communities. A large tree was uprooted and fell into the road in one Royal Palm Beach neighborhood, blocking traffic. Firefighters responded and pulled the tree from the road so neighbors could clear it. Hail pelted cars, lightning struck close to residents and strong winds caused widespread damage throughout the area.

Seven-year-old Danny Jaworski was home with his grandmother when the storm hit. Danny and his grandmother watched as the massive tree came down in front of a car driving down their street, blocking the road. Danny's mother, Leslie Jaworski, owns the home, which had been named the neighborhood's Home of the Month. She was at work when the storm hit and came home to find firefighters already on scene working to clear the tree. Leslie said she was grateful the tree did not land on her roof and that traffic was able to get through. As a new homeowner, the experience has her worried about future storms and what can happen.

cards.headline: Boca Raton's George Snow Scholarship Fund awards record $7.5 million to 470 students
cards.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded a record $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County, according to President Tim Snow. The program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford by offering four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college.

Beyond financial assistance, the fund provides mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast, said Vice President of Development Jay Brandt. One 2026 recipient, Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate planning to attend Georgetown University, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship. The fund's expanded services include the Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, which offers professional, formal, and casual wear donated by the community to help scholars prepare for interviews, internships, and campus life.

cards.headline: West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade offers trade certifications to residents
cards.teaser: West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade provides programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and other trades to help high school students and adults get trained and certified for work.
cards.body:
West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade offers trade certifications through programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and more. Adrian Dowdell with the education center said West Tech is appropriate for high school students and adults looking to learn a trade and get certifications that lead to work.

The center works with community and business partners to help people find work in Belle Glade and surrounding communities. During a recent Let's Hear It meet-up at the Belle Glade library, WPTV Morning Anchor Ashley Glass connected with the people behind West Technical Education Center, who brought a giant truck to spread the word about their programs. Those interested in learning more can email LetsHearIt@wptv.com.

hero.headline: Boca Raton's George Snow Scholarship Fund awards record $7.5 million to 470 students
hero.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund has achieved a record-breaking milestone in 2026, distributing more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to students across Palm Beach and Broward counties.
hero.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund in Boca Raton has distributed more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students throughout Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026. President Tim Snow announced the record-breaking milestone to WPTV. Over its four-decade history, the nonprofit organization has awarded more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, establishing itself as the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. The fund's core mission focuses on addressing the gap between traditional financial aid packages and what students and their families can realistically afford. Scholarship recipients receive four-year commitments, which Snow said helps provide financial stability throughout their college years.

The organization's support extends well beyond monetary scholarships. Vice President of Development Jay Brandt emphasized that GSSF offers mentorship, professional development opportunities, and educational resources including the College Compass podcast. These comprehensive services are designed to give scholars the tools they need to succeed academically and professionally. Among the 2026 recipients is Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate who earned two scholarships: the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship. Chow plans to attend Georgetown University and expressed her appreciation for the organization's support.

One distinctive program within GSSF is the Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, directed by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine. The boutique provides professional, formal, and casual clothing to help scholars prepare for important life transitions. Students can access appropriate wear for job interviews, internships, and their first days on campus. The boutique receives donations of both new and gently used clothing along with footwear and accessories from the community.

The George Snow Scholarship Fund's comprehensive approach to student support reflects growing recognition that removing financial barriers alone is insufficient for true educational equity. As college costs continue rising, organizations like GSSF are addressing multiple dimensions of student success. By combining financial aid with mentorship, professional development, and practical resources like clothing for interviews and campus life, the fund tackles obstacles that often prevent capable students from underserved communities from reaching their full potential. The organization's 2026 results demonstrate that South Florida communities continue to invest in the next generation's educational opportunities.

cards.headline: Florida Mango Festival brings 75 vendors, rare varieties to West Palm Beach this Saturday
cards.teaser: The Florida Mango Festival will take place Saturday, June 27, at the Palm Beach County Convention Center at 650 Okeechobee Blvd.
cards.body:
The Florida Mango Festival will take place Saturday, June 27, at the Palm Beach County Convention Center at 650 Okeechobee Blvd. in West Palm Beach. The event will feature more than 75 vendors serving local mango varieties, grafted trees, tropical fruits, and mango-themed products. Festival co-organizer Vince Rogers highlighted some of the state's most unique varieties, including Fruit Cocktail, a sweet, multi-layered flavor; Orange Sherbet, offering creamy citrus notes; and Pineapple Pleasure, with tropical pineapple undertones. Florida hosts more than 350 mango varieties far beyond what's typically available in grocery stores. Alex Salazar of Tropical Acres Farms said the indoor, air-conditioned venue offers an ideal setting for people to taste, learn, and discover Florida-grown mangoes without worrying about the summer heat.

Throughout the day, visitors can attend educational talks on home mango growing and grafting techniques. Salazar will lead demonstrations offering tips for both beginners and seasoned growers. Additional features include an ID Your Mango booth, a scion exchange for online mango community members, and a master display of Florida's diverse mango cultivars. The festival starts at 10:30 a.m., with first pick ticket holders entering at 9 a.m. Garage parking is included with ticket purchase but availability is limited. Paid public parking is available nearby north of Okeechobee Blvd. Tickets and more information are available at floridamangofestival.com.

cards.headline: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League urges pet hurricane prep as season progresses
cards.teaser: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create a disaster plan for their pets before the next storm hits.
cards.body:
With hurricane season in full swing, Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create a disaster plan for their pets before the next storm hits. Dr. Alyssa Comroe, CEO of Peggy Adams, told WPTV the safest place for pets during a hurricane is right alongside their owners. The shelter's expert team recommends several key steps for pet safety, starting with microchipping and identification. Pets should wear a collar with current identification and have an updated microchip registered with correct contact information.

The shelter also advises introducing pets to a designated safe room ahead of time, such as a walk-in closet or downstairs bathroom, and conducting practice runs so the hurricane isn't their first time there. Residents should prepare a pet emergency kit with a three-day supply of food and water in airtight containers, bowls, a sturdy carrier, bedding, towels, medications for two weeks, vaccination records, first-aid supplies, litter and box for cats, leashes, harnesses, cool packs, wipes, waste bags, and multiple forms of visible ID. Additionally, keep a printed list of local pet-friendly shelters and hotels accessible and maintain recent photos of pets ideally with their owner to help with identification if separated. Florida's hurricane season runs June through November, overlapping with extreme summer heat.

hero.headline: DeSantis vetoes bills on e-bike safety tracking and teen poll workers despite unanimous legislative support
hero.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis rejected two bipartisan bills that passed the Legislature with unanimous votes, including one that would have created a statewide system for tracking e-bike and scooter crashes.
hero.body:
Ron DeSantis vetoed Senate Bill 382 and House Bill 461 just before 8 p.m. Thursday, rejecting two bipartisan measures that passed the Legislature with unanimous votes earlier this year. SB 382, filed by Republican Sen. Keith Truenow, sought to create a statewide system for tracking e-bike and scooter crashes. Currently, local and state agencies record these incidents differently, leaving no consistent data for policymakers to assess the scale of the problem. The legislation would have established a task force to deliver recommendations by Oct. 1 on regulating micromobility devices. The bill also aimed to cap e-bike speeds at 10 miles per hour on sidewalks when pedestrians are nearby and require riders to yield on shared paths, with violations treated as non-criminal traffic infractions. DeSantis' veto comes weeks after an Orlando boy was killed on his e-scooter in Lake Nona when the 13-year-old cut in front of a truck while picking up flowers for Mother's Day.

DeSantis also rejected HB 461, which would have allowed high school students to volunteer as poll workers in exchange for community service hours for graduation requirements or Bright Futures scholarships. The bill, sponsored by Republican Reps. Kiyan Michael and Susan Valdés, would have loosened rules on privately funded election-related expenses to allow students to volunteer at polls before the August Primary. The measure was backed by the League of Women Voters and the Southern Poverty Law Center. The Governor additionally vetoed HB 4075, a local bill for the town of Davie in Broward County, sponsored by Democrat Rep. Michael Gottlieb, that would have exempted agricultural land from outdoor advertising laws.

cards.headline: Judge sets July 29 hearing on challenge to DeSantis property tax ballot language
cards.teaser: A Leon County judge is fast-tracking a lawsuit that challenges the wording of Governor Ron DeSantis's property tax constitutional amendment before counties begin printing ballots for the General Election.
cards.body:
Circuit Judge Angela Dempsey has set a July 29 hearing for a lawsuit challenging the ballot language of Gov. Ron DeSantis' property tax amendment. The case, filed by Save Our Voters From Misleading Ballot Language and joined by former Stuart Mayor Thomas Campenni and former Key Biscayne Mayor Michael Davey, disputes the wording of the proposed constitutional amendment. The plaintiffs argue that the ballot summary promises to ensure funding for core services, but the amendment would actually require local governments to spend whatever property tax revenue remains on public safety, schools, infrastructure, and natural resources. According to the lawsuit, by substantially reducing the local property tax base, the amendment is likely to decrease revenues available to local governments to fund core services.

Lawmakers passed House Joint Resolution 1F during this month's Special Session, placing the measure on the ballot. If approved by at least 60% of voters, the amendment would raise the nonschool homestead exemption to $150,000 starting Jan. 1, 2027, and to $250,000 the following year. It would also cut the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead property from 10% to 5%. State analysts estimate the proposal would shrink local property tax collections by almost $5 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year, with yearly impact rising to more than $10.7 billion by 2030-31. DeSantis defends the ballot summary, noting that lawmakers amended state law to allow more explanatory language than the usual 75-word limit.

cards.headline: Trump approval rating drops underwater in Florida as midterms approach
cards.teaser: New polling shows 52% of Florida voters now view President Donald Trump unfavorably, compared to 46% who see him positively, a ten-point swing from January.
cards.body:
New polling from Global Strategy Group shows President Donald Trump's approval rating has dropped significantly in Florida. The latest numbers show 52% of Florida voters view Trump unfavorably compared to 46% who view him positively, marking a ten-point swing from January when he held a +4 net approval rating. He now sits at -6. The poll was released by Democratic Senate candidate Alex Vindman's campaign as he argues Florida could be competitive when U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody faces voters in November. According to a GSG polling memo, this double-digit decline in Trump's popularity has created a more favorable political environment for Democrats in 2026.

Trump is losing support within his own base. Since January, support among White college-aged voters has dropped 15 points, while registered Republicans have seen a net 10-point decline in approval. Even among self-identified Trump 2024 voters, his numbers are down 10 points. The trend extends beyond Florida. GSG found Trump's approval underwater in Ohio, where he sits at 41% approval and 53% disapproval, and in Texas at 41% to 54%. In May, the same pollster found Moody holding a 46% to 43% lead over Vindman, within the poll's 3.1% margin of error. For comparison, in 2018, the last midterm during Trump's presidency, exit polls showed he remained popular in Florida despite national unpopularity.

cards.headline: Democratic campaign committee attacks Rep. Salazar for missing housing bill vote after mother's death
cards.teaser: The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee criticized U.S. Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar for touting support of a bipartisan housing bill after she missed the vote due to her mother's death.
cards.body:
Rep. María Elvira Salazar celebrated the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (HR 6644), which cleared the House on a 358-32 vote. The South Florida Republican posted on Facebook that housing costs are one of the biggest concerns she hears about and that she supported the bipartisan legislation. However, Salazar missed the vote and all votes cast that week because of her mother's death. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee quickly pointed out the missed vote, with spokesperson Madison Andrus stating that if Salazar is misleading her constituents and taking credit for votes she could not be bothered to show up for, then Miamians will replace her with a real leader who will fight for their ability to afford housing.

Salazar's office provided a statement saying she had helped shape the bill through the legislative process and consistently supported the legislation. The statement notes that Salazar voted for the bill in the House Financial Services Committee and twice on the House floor to advance it to the Senate. The final package includes her RESIDE Act, which she originally released in September and identified as one of her signature housing priorities. President Donald Trump was expected to sign the legislation at an event on Capitol Hill this week but canceled it amid a fight with the Senate over an election reform bill. The DCCC identified Salazar's seat among Florida's "Districts in Play" for the 2026 election cycle.

cards.headline: Republican Party of Florida announces speaker lineup for Sunshine Summit without full gubernatorial debate
cards.teaser: The Republican Party of Florida announced speakers for its Sunshine Summit event, featuring most gubernatorial candidates separately rather than in a unified debate format.
cards.body:
The Republican Party of Florida announced its speaker lineup for the Sunshine Summit, which will feature most major GOP gubernatorial candidates speaking separately rather than in a joint debate. Republican Party of Florida Chair Evan Power said the event "will showcase the Florida leadership that has made Florida the conservative beacon of freedom" and emphasized the importance of showcasing future leadership ahead of November elections. The gubernatorial candidates scheduled to speak include Jay Collins, Byron Donalds, Paul Renner and Bobby Williams.

The speaker list also includes congressional leaders U.S. Sens. Ashley Moody and Rick Scott, U.S. Reps. Kat Cammack and Mario Díaz-Balart, and members of Florida's Cabinet: Attorney General James Uthmeier, Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia and Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson. State legislators Erin Grall, Dean Black, Jennifer Canady and Meg Weinberger will have featured spots, along with education activist Erika Donalds and Education Commissioner Stasi Kamoutsas. The event will feature two congressional debates moderated by Axios White House reporter Marc Caputo and POLITICO Florida Playbook Editor Kim Leonard for the Republican primaries in Florida's 19th and 25th Congressional Districts, with confirmed candidates including Madison Cawthorn, Ola Hawatmeh and Catalina Lauf in CD 19, and Dan Franzese, Raven Harrison, George Moraitis and Scott Singer in CD 25.

cards.headline: DeSantis highlights Alligator Alcatraz immigration detention facility
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis highlighted the success of Alligator Alcatraz and Florida's continued efforts in combatting illegal immigration.
cards.body:
DeSantis released a statement through the Executive Office of the Governor highlighting the operation of Alligator Alcatraz, the state's immigration detention facility, and Florida's continued efforts in combatting illegal immigration. The facility has been part of the state's immigration enforcement strategy under the DeSantis administration.

The Governor's office emphasized Florida's role in immigration enforcement as the Trump administration moves forward with deportation policies. The statement comes as the Supreme Court has cleared the way for the administration to end temporary protected status for migrants from multiple countries, including Haiti and Syria, which would particularly impact Florida given its large population of TPS holders.

hero.headline: Palm City resident Lee Hayes dies
hero.teaser: Lee Hayes of Palm City has died. Services are being handled by Forest Hills Memorial Park & Palm City Chapel.
hero.body:
Lee Hayes of Palm City has died, according to an obituary published Friday. The Palm City resident's death was announced through Forest Hills Memorial Park & Palm City Chapel.

Funeral arrangements are being handled by Forest Hills Memorial Park & Palm City Chapel in Palm City. The obituary was published Friday morning for the Martin County resident.

cards.headline: Martin County water plant crash disrupts service after driver flees scene
cards.teaser: A crash at a Martin County water plant Thursday disrupted water service after the driver fled the scene.
cards.body:
A crash at a Martin County water plant Thursday disrupted water service after the driver fled the scene. The Martin County Sheriff's Office identified the driver who crashed into the water plant facility before leaving the area.

The crash occurred Thursday evening at the Martin County water treatment facility. Officials said the driver left the scene following the collision with the plant infrastructure. Water service to customers was affected by the incident.

Martin County authorities worked to identify and locate the driver who fled after the crash. The collision caused damage to the water plant that required immediate response from county utilities staff. Service disruptions impacted residents supplied by the affected facility.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office successfully identified the driver after investigating the hit and run crash. Officials did not immediately provide details on the extent of damage to the water plant or how long service disruptions would last for affected customers.

cards.headline: OnPoint Mobile Injections brings regenerative cell therapy to Stuart
cards.teaser: A mobile medical service is expanding access to regenerative cell therapy in Stuart.
cards.body:
OnPoint Mobile Injections announced Friday it is expanding access to regenerative cell therapy in Stuart. The company provides mobile medical services to Martin County residents.

The Stuart expansion brings regenerative cell therapy treatments directly to patients in Martin County. OnPoint Mobile Injections specializes in providing medical procedures at patient locations rather than requiring office visits.

cards.headline: Four recommended restaurants in Stuart and Jensen Beach highlighted
cards.teaser: A dining guide features favorite restaurants in Stuart and Jensen Beach for Martin County residents.
cards.body:
Four Florida restaurants in Stuart and Jensen Beach were featured Friday in a local dining guide. The restaurants represent favorite dining options in the two Martin County communities.

The guide highlights eating establishments in Stuart and Jensen Beach for residents and visitors. Both towns are located in Martin County along the Treasure Coast.

cards.headline: Orlando Health opens new primary care center in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: Orlando Health cut the ribbon Thursday on a new eight-exam room adult primary health care center in Vero Beach to address doctor shortages in Indian River County.
cards.body:
Orlando Health held a ribbon cutting Thursday for a new eight-exam room adult primary health care center in Vero Beach located at 3745 11th Circle Suite 101. Aaron Bridges, assistant vice president of Orlando Health, said the facility can see 40 patients per day with opportunity to grow. The Orlando Health Physician Associates Adult Medicine center will be led by husband-and-wife physicians Dr. Meron Kristos and Dr. Gabitto, who met during residency at the former St. Vincent's hospital in New York City.

Both physicians said primary care access is limited in Indian River County and throughout Florida. According to the Cleveland Clinic, Indian River County is designated a health professional shortage area and medically underserved area. Dr. Kristos noted that people in the area are waiting months and months for appointments. Christine Stenback, who moved to Indian River County nearly three decades ago, said the shortage has been a persistent problem since her arrival. She said she and her daughter had to retain doctors in Fort Lauderdale and travel back for specialist care, an issue she said has never really changed.

cards.headline: Spirit Airlines bankruptcy leaves Treasure Coast travelers with fewer low-cost options
cards.teaser: The end of Spirit Airlines raises questions about the future of budget air travel for Treasure Coast residents as the carrier enters bankruptcy court.
cards.body:
Spirit Airlines has entered bankruptcy court to sell off its assets, including planes, airport gates and potentially its headquarters. Clint Henderson, managing editor of news at The Points Guy travel website, said these assets could be valuable and likely go to the highest bidder. The deadline for bids on Spirit's assets comes in July.

A Treasure Coast entrepreneur, LeRoy Gillead II, has proposed buying all of Spirit and rebranding it as Florida Air Express, a low-cost airline based in West Palm Beach. According to court papers, Gillead is looking to raise as much as $250 million from private investors. However, Henderson expressed skepticism about the proposal, saying "This seems like a pie in the sky thing" and noting that the proposed airline does not currently fly any routes. Henderson said it is more likely that Spirit's assets will be divided among major airlines. Henderson also noted that low-cost carriers are struggling in the United States, with Frontier and Allegiant remaining in the low-cost category. He advised travelers to search for cheap fares across multiple airlines using Google Flights rather than remaining loyal to one carrier.

cards.headline: Delray Beach food truck owner calls mother's Venezuela earthquake survival a miracle
cards.teaser: Josney Peroza, who owns Ukelele Foods and operates a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, says his mother survived two powerful earthquakes that struck Venezuela.
cards.body:
Josney Peroza, owner of Ukelele Foods, a Venezuelan food truck operating in Delray Beach, learned of two earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes that struck Venezuela seconds apart. After seeing a video showing the building where his mother lived had collapsed, Peroza spent hours unable to contact her as power outages and blocked communications made connections nearly impossible. About eight hours after the collapse, he received a call after 3 a.m. confirming his mother was alive under the rubble. Relatives and neighbors worked with their bare hands to free her from the debris.

Peroza said his mother has a broken hip, needs surgery and lost her home in the collapse. He described a wider humanitarian crisis in the coastal state of La Guaira, where residents have no power, water or homes. He said Venezuela was not prepared for a disaster of this scale and needs immediate international help. Most buildings are made of concrete and metal, making rescue efforts with limited tools nearly impossible. Officials confirm nearly 200 people are dead and at least 1,000 others are hurt. Peroza said he plans to help his mother from Florida rather than traveling to the disaster zone, where there is no commercial activity or work available.

hero.headline: Massive waterfront hotel project reinvented in Fort Pierce
hero.teaser: A major waterfront hotel development in Fort Pierce has been redesigned.
hero.body:
A massive waterfront hotel project in Fort Pierce has been reinvented. The development is planned for the Fort Pierce waterfront area.

The project represents a significant redesign of earlier plans for the site. The hotel development is among the largest hospitality projects proposed for Fort Pierce.

Details about the revised project scope and timeline are being finalized.

cards.headline: Jocelyne L. Bonnet of Fort Pierce dies

cards.body:
Jocelyne L. Bonnet of Fort Pierce has died. Stone Brothers Funeral Home in Fort Pierce announced the death on Thursday.

Bonnet was a Fort Pierce resident. Stone Brothers Funeral Home is located in Fort Pierce and serves St. Lucie County families.

The funeral home has published the obituary notice. Further details about services will be provided by the funeral home.

cards.headline: Sailing yacht Legacy worth $16 million sinks in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: A sailing yacht valued at $16 million has sunk in Fort Pierce waters.
cards.body:
The sailing yacht Legacy, valued at $16 million, has sunk in Fort Pierce. The vessel went down in Fort Pierce waters.

The yacht named Legacy was a sailing vessel of significant value. The sinking occurred in the Fort Pierce area.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie prank with toy gun leads to armed confrontation and arrests
cards.teaser: A prank involving a toy gun in Port St. Lucie escalated to an armed confrontation and resulted in arrests.
cards.body:
A prank involving a toy gun in Port St. Lucie led to an armed confrontation and arrests. The incident occurred in Port St. Lucie.

The toy gun prank escalated into a serious situation involving weapons. Port St. Lucie police responded to the confrontation.

Arrests were made following the incident. The confrontation stemmed from the initial prank with the toy gun.

cards.headline: Major crash blocks lanes on I-95 North near Gatlin Boulevard in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: A major crash on I-95 North near Gatlin Boulevard in St. Lucie County is blocking multiple lanes.
cards.body:

cards.headline: Orlando Health opens eight-room primary care center in Vero Beach to address physician shortage
cards.teaser: Orlando Health held a ribbon cutting Thursday for a new eight-exam room adult primary health care center in Vero Beach.
cards.body:
Orlando Health held a ribbon cutting Thursday for a new eight-exam room adult primary health care center in Vero Beach located at 3745 11th Circle Suite 101. The facility can serve 40 patients a day and has opportunity to grow, according to Aaron Bridges, assistant vice president of Orlando Health. The center will be led by husband-and-wife physicians Dr. Meron Kristos and Dr. Gabitto, who met in residency at the former St. Vincent's hospital in New York City.

Both doctors said primary care access is limited in Indian River County and throughout Florida. According to the Cleveland Clinic, Indian River is designated a health professional shortage area and medically underserved area. Kristos noted the shortage leads to longer wait times for patients. "People are waiting months and months," Kristos said. Christine Stenback, who moved to Indian River County nearly three decades ago, said she has experienced the shortage firsthand, retaining doctors in Fort Lauderdale and traveling back for specialist care. Kristos hopes the new facility can reduce wait times and provide more access to health care. "We're able to provide as a quick timeframe to see us to get established, and then when something pops up, you have somebody to go see," Kristos said.
